title: Placement-driven reversal of preferred spin alignment in monolayer hBN vacancy pairs
abstract: The negatively charged boron vacancy is an optically addressable spin centre in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), but bringing two vacancies together introduces electronic interactions absent from the isolated-defect picture. Here we use density-functional theory at total charge q = -2 to show that atomic-scale placement reverses the preferred collinear spin alignment in monolayer hBN. Among seven configurations, the closest pair, separated by 4.3 angstrom, favours parallel alignment by 27.6 meV within the semilocal approximation. Moving one vacancy by a single lattice vector reverses the preference, and a 7.5 angstrom pair favours antiparallel alignment by 50.7 meV. Numerical controls change these two reference splittings by less than 1 meV; hybrid-functional calculations retain their signs while substantially changing their magnitudes. Local distortions connect the antiparallel preference at 7.5 angstrom to changes in vacancy-state hybridization along an intervening atomic chain. The closest pair instead exhibits a contact-localized spin-density contrast and constrained angular energies that depart from the bilinear Heisenberg form. These results identify a placement-sensitive regime of interacting defects and provide a microscopic foundation for investigating coupled spin centres in atomically thin materials.
summary: This theoretical study uses DFT to map out how the spin alignment preference between two interacting vacancies in monolayer hBN is dictated by their precise atomic placement. The results show that small structural changes can reverse the preferred spin coupling, indicating a complex, placement-sensitive electronic interaction regime. This work establishes a key physical principle for engineering coupled spin qubits in 2D materials.
main_problem: The study investigates how the electronic interactions between two closely placed, negatively charged boron vacancies in monolayer hBN reverse the preferred collinear spin alignment based on their atomic-scale placement.
main_result: The spin alignment preference is highly placement-sensitive, with the sign of the energy splitting reversing when the vacancies are shifted by a single lattice vector, demonstrating a departure from simple bilinear Heisenberg models.
method: Density-Functional Theory (DFT) calculations are used to compute the energy difference ($\Delta E$) between parallel and antiparallel spin alignments for various vacancy configurations.
model_or_system: The system is a monolayer of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) containing two negatively charged boron vacancies ($	ext{V}^-$). Calculations are performed using DFT at a total charge $q=-2$ across seven different atomic placements.
key_observables: Energy splitting ($\Delta E$) between parallel (P) and antiparallel (AP) states, spin-density contrast, and the dependence of $\Delta E$ on vacancy separation and relative placement.
important_parameters: The closest pair (4.3 Å) favors parallel alignment by $27.6 	ext{ meV}$, while a 7.5 Å pair favors antiparallel alignment by $50.7 	ext{ meV}$. The splitting is significantly larger than the isolated-center zero-field splitting.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on collinear Kohn–Sham solutions, which are not guaranteed to represent true quantum multiplets, and the comparison is sensitive to the choice of DFT functional (PBE vs. HSE06).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate atomic placement effects, $\Delta E$ vs. separation, and spin-density isosurfaces for specific vacancy configurations, while tables summarize the calculated energy splittings for multiple placements.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the placement dependence of spin alignment using DFT, comparing results across different separations and structural motifs (e.g., chain vs. contact modes) to establish a placement-sensitive regime for interacting defects.
why_interesting: This work provides a microscopic, first-principles foundation for understanding coupled spin centers in atomically thin materials, which is crucial for designing next-generation quantum devices based on solid-state defects.
